Core Finding

Resistance training improves muscle strength, hypertrophy, power, endurance, contraction velocity, and physical
function in healthy adults.

However, only a few prescription variables significantly enhance adaptations beyond the
basic effect of doing RT versus doing nothing.

Notably, load magnitude does not consistently impact hypertrophyâ€”low loads
(30% 1RM) to high loads (100% 1RM) produce similar gains when effort is near-fatiguing.
Power RT also enhances physical function outcomes.

Equipment type (machines vs free weights), exercise complexity (single-joint vs multi-joint),
set structure (cluster, drop sets, complex, contrast), time under tension, blood flow restriction, and periodization do not
consistently impact training outcomes when volume and effort are equated.
These are clinically relevant outcomes for aging populations and rehabilitation settings.

The
evidence confirms that lower extremity strength training is a primary driver of functional independence.

Safety Profile of RT
æŠ—é˜»è®​ç»ƒçš„å®‰å…¨æ€§

RT is safe for healthy adults of all ages.

Analysis of >38,000 participants showed no increased risk of serious adverse
events from exercise.

Non-fatal cardiovascular complications occur much less frequently during RT than aerobic
training.
Musculoskeletal complications are rare and typically resolve by adjusting intensity or body position.

Isokinetic RT provides constant-velocity resistance that adapts to the user's force output, enabling maximal muscle
tension throughout the full joint range.

This aligns with the evidence that complete ROM and safe, controlled loading
are key to strength development.

The ability to quantify muscle function data (e.g., peak force, power, work, RFD) and
provide real-time feedback supports evidence-based, individualized prescriptionâ€”consistent with the review's
emphasis on individualization to maximize adherence and effectiveness.

Weekly frequencies as low as 2 sessions,
volumes as low as 2â€“3 sets per exercise, and loads across the full spectrum (30%â€“100% 1RM) are all effective.

The
review concludes that prioritizing participation and adherence is more important than conforming to specific
prescription criteria.

An accessible, safe, and efficient training system that users will actually use repeatedly may
deliver greater real-world benefit than an optimal theoretical protocol with poor adherence.
